newsitem.title: SPAIN: Fall in Spanish Bonos seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Fall in Spanish Bonos seen limited.

text.p: A selloff in Spanish debt triggered by fears Spain may not join the first wave of European Monetary Union should be contained by both strong domestic demand and the government's firm commitment to fiscal austerity, analysts said on Tuesday.

The 10-year spread of bonos over Bunds has widened to 106 basis points from a record low of 83 at the end of January as doubts surfaced about Spain's chances of qualifying for the launch of a single European currency in 1999.

"Even in the worst case scenario, with Spain entering in the second wave of the European Monetary Union, I do not think the spread over Bunds should increase more than 20 basis points," said Mark Geddes, economist at 4CAST in London.
Remarks from German politicians and bankers at the weekend held out the prospect of turmoil on financial markets if peripheral countries like Italy join EMU from the start.

The debt markets of so-called "Club Med" countries -- Italy, Spain and Portugal -- were all punished as foreign investors realised the holy grail of qualifying for EMU may still be out of their reach.
"Spain is still vulnerable to bad news from Italy. This is a risk which the market is starting to take on board," said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Market in London.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government has focused the nation's EMU drive on economic accomplishments in an attempt to dissociate Spain from the more politically powerful but economically weak-kneed Italy.
Spain offers better performance in terms of public deficit and debt than Italy and is trying to distinguish bonos from Italian Btps in the minds of investors.
Though foreigners may be nervous bonos are not offering enough value to counterbalance the political risk of Spain being left out of the EMU, analysts remained calm.
They see little chance of Spain abandoning its rigourous fiscal policy or letting down its guard on inflation which is approaching 3.0 percent.
Also, analysts predicted the Bank of Spain will end 1997 with its key money market rate below the current six percent level.
Experts are confident Spain's sound economic fundamentals will limit potential bond losses. Analysts put resistance on the 10-year bonos spread over Bunds at around 120.
Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said on Tuesday that joining EMU would depend on meeting the Maastricht Treaty criteria and not on political statements or opinions.

But the change in sentiment was apparent to analysts who said a decline in the peseta was evidence foreign investors were taking profits amassed during most of 1996 in peripheral markets and moving back into core markets.
Despite almost continuous intervention by the Bank of Spain since last Thursday, the peseta was trading on Tuesday at 84.84/86 per mark, far from its peak of 83.30 in mid-January.
Peseta weakness limits the scope for rate cuts in the near term.
"Of course the pressure to cut rates is less than it was in the past," said Valentin Fernandez at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

Reduced expectations for easing were reflected in a flattening of the yield curve, with the spread between the two- and 10-year bonds declining from around 150 basis points in mid-January to around 120 b.p.s on Tuesday.
However, the peseta's decline should not hinder easing later in the year. Dealers were still expecting to end the year with a repo rate around 5.0 percent.

Strong domestic demand is also offering support to the debt market. Domestic investors are moving money increasingly from low-yield or interest-free bank deposits to financial assets, dealers in Madrid said.

"We had a change in sentiment, especially from foreigners. But what is really supporting the market is a pretty high demand by mutual and pension funds," said a senior dealer at a U.S. investment house in Madrid who asked not to be named.
